To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of antibacterial products is not associated with increased resistance of environmental bacteria in the home to antibiotics or to antibacterial agents.

there was a significant association between antibiotic resistance in bacteria from the homes of antibacterial users and nonusers, and that this association was stronger in the case of bacteria that were resistant to multiple antibiotics than for single‐drug resistant isolates.

the use of antibacterial agents in the home is associated with an increased prevalence of antibiotic and antibacterially cross‐resistant target bacteria in the home environment, and this is associated with increased antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates from the same region.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following objectives: (1) to determine the relationship between resistance in clinical and environmental bacteria, (2) to determine the impact of the use of antibacterial products on the resistance profiles of environmental bacteria, (3) to determine the prevalence of antibiotic resistance in environmental bacteria, and (4) to determine the presence of genes encoding resistance to antibiotics and antibacterial agents in environmental bacteria.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of antibacterial agents in the environment, including the home, is associated with an increased risk of cross‐resistance to antibiotics in target organisms, and that this risk is greater in the home environment than in the hospital environment.
there is a lack of data on which to draw any conclusions regarding the relationship between antibiotic resistance, antibacterial agent resistance, and the use of household antibacterial products.
there is no evidence that antibacterial products contribute to the selection of resistant organisms in the home environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there was no evidence that the presence of antibacterial agents in the home was associated with increased antibiotic resistance in the bacteria we tested.
we have found that there is a relationship between antibacterial resistance and the use of antibacterial products.

we are able to demonstrate that there is no significant correlation between the use of antibacterial products in the home and the prevalence of antibiotic resistance genes in bacteria isolated from the home environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antibacterial product users have more resistant bacteria in their home environments.
the presence of antibacterial agents in the environment can be associated with the selection of antibiotic resistance in environmental bacteria.

the presence of antibacterial agents in the home does not appear to be a major factor in selecting for antibiotic or antibacterial agent resistance in target organisms, and that the presence or absence of antibacterial products in the home does little to change the resistance profiles of these organisms.
